title: Purim: masks
hook: costumes hint at hidden faces, as God is hidden in Esther

segments.voice: Yesterday, matanot la'evyonim. Your line was two gifts to the poor. Did your two gifts reach two people? Today, the costumes, and what hides behind them. Day six hundred seventy-five.

Start with an absence. The book of Esther, a book of the Hebrew Bible, read aloud in synagogues every year, never mentions God. Not once. In the Hebrew text, there's no prayer, no prophet, no angel, no miracle that a camera could film. A queen, a minister, a king who can't sleep, a lucky coincidence, and then another. The Greek version of the book, made in ancient times, adds prayers. But in the Hebrew, the silence stays. And Purim's costumes, some teachers say, are a way of dressing up in that silence.
screen: `A BIBLE BOOK WITHOUT GOD'S NAME.` → `NO PRAYER, NO PROPHET, NO ANGEL.` → `DRESSING UP IN THE SILENCE.`

segments.voice: The Talmud plays with this. In tractate Chullin, the rabbis ask a riddle: where is Esther hinted at in the Torah? And they answer with a verse from Deuteronomy, where God says, in the old Jewish translation, "And I will surely hide My face in that day." In Hebrew, I will surely hide is haster astir. Hear the sound? Haster. Esther. The name of the book sounds like hiding. Esther herself is hidden, too. When she's taken to the palace, she doesn't tell anyone she's Jewish; Mordecai told her not to. The Talmud, in Megillah, even says she was called Esther because she concealed who she was. Her face is in the palace; her identity is under a mask. And the whole story runs on things that look like chance: a sleepless king who happens to have the royal chronicles read to him, and happens to hear about Mordecai saving his life. Jewish tradition reads those coincidences as God working behind the curtain. Not absent. Hidden. Wearing costumes on Purim is a much later custom, usually traced to Jews in Italy, where a rabbi allowed it as part of the day's joy. Explanations came afterward, and one that teachers give is this: on Purim, everyone looks like someone else, because in the story, nothing was quite what it seemed. The queen was hiding who she was. The coincidences were hiding a hand. A mask asks the same question every time someone opens the door: who's really under there?
screen: `HASTER ASTIR: I WILL HIDE.` · `ESTHER HIDES WHO SHE IS.` · `COINCIDENCES, OR A HAND?` · `COSTUMES: ITALY, LATE 1400S.` · then, large: `WHO'S UNDER THE MASK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what's under a mask. Breathe, and think of someone you saw this week who seemed fine. Cheerful at work, funny in the group chat, put together at pickup. Now imagine, gently, what might be under that: tiredness, worry, a loss they haven't mentioned. You don't need to guess right. Then turn it toward yourself. What's one thing you've been hiding behind the words, I'm fine? Just name it, quietly. The bell holds the time.
Purim. Lots, and a story where God's name is hidden and the costumes remind us to look underneath. Today's word.
Your line: who's under the mask. Today, ask one person how they're really doing, and wait long enough for the real answer. Day six hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: On Purim, many Jews, especially children, wear costumes to hear the Megillah and to the festive meal; the custom is described as part of the day's joy, and some teachers connect it to the hidden ways God works in the book of Esther.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): removed the late-1400s date (claims rule; now "usually traced to Jews in Italy") from voice and games, removed the guessed motive for the Greek additions, softened "many teachers", fixed the garbled "hiding behind a fine".

God's name absent from Hebrew Esther; the Greek Additions to Esther include prayers of Mordecai and Esther. Factual, stated without ranking.

Costume custom: first attested in late 15th-century Italy; Rabbi Judah Minz (d. 1508) is usually cited as permitting it. Verify.
